reference_text:
Welcome to the course. We will work through each concept carefully, connect the
ideas step by step, and use practical examples to make technical topics easier
to understand. When we introduce a new method, focus first on the problem it
solves and why it is useful. For example, in machine learning, features are the
information we give the model, while the target is what we want it to predict.
Now consider a simple question: what changes when the data contains missing
values? We will think through the reason and then look at the code. In Python,
we can inspect the data, run one small step at a time, and explain what the
result means. The goal is to understand the logic, not simply memorize syntax.

slides.title: Big picture
slides.transcript:
Welcome to Module 6, Joining Data in PostgreSQL. Up to this point, many of our examples have focused on one table at a time. That is useful for learning SQL, but real projects rarely stay inside one table. A hospital may store patient demographics in one table, admissions in another, lab tests in another, and staff information somewhere else. A university may separate students, courses, registrations, and grades. An online store may separate customers, orders, products, and payments. To answer useful questions, we often need to bring those pieces together.

The important skill in this module is not just memorizing JOIN syntax. I want you to think about what the final rows mean. If one patient has three admissions, should that patient appear once or three times? If a patient has no admissions, should the patient disappear or remain? Those questions determine the join strategy. This same reasoning applies whether you are joining hospital data, customer data, student records, or financial transactions.

[tts-break]

We will work with INNER, LEFT, RIGHT, and FULL OUTER joins, but we will also go beyond the basic definitions. We will compare ON and WHERE, use self joins and cross joins, and spend time on cardinality because row multiplication can quietly create incorrect counts.

As you move through the module, try to predict the output before you run the SQL. Then run the query and compare your prediction with the result. That habit is extremely useful in real analytics work because a query can run successfully and still answer the wrong question. In a real project, a wrong join can change a dashboard, a report, or even a decision, so understanding the meaning of the rows is more important than simply getting a green execution message.

slides.title: Learning objectives
slides.transcript:
By the end of this module, you should be able to choose a join type based on the business question, not simply because one join looks familiar. When someone says, show me only customers who placed an order, that suggests one type of join. When they say, show me every customer, including those with no orders, that suggests another. SQL becomes easier when you translate the wording of the question into a rule about which rows must remain.

You will also practice using table aliases. When two or three tables contain columns with similar names, aliases keep the query readable. Instead of wondering which patient_id we mean, we can make the source explicit. You should also become comfortable reading a join from left to right and explaining each table's role in plain language.

[tts-break]

A major goal is understanding grain. Grain means what one row represents. One row might represent one patient, one admission, one lab test, one order, or one department. If you expect one row per patient but your query returns ten rows for one patient, that may be a warning sign. On the other hand, if the result is supposed to be one row per admission, repeated patient names may be completely correct.

Finally, you should be able to validate a join. We will compare row counts, distinct IDs, unmatched records, and known examples. In real projects, validation is not optional. A join that looks visually reasonable can still produce inflated counts or silently remove important records. By the end, I want you to be able to defend not only the SQL syntax, but also why the result represents the population and grain that the question actually requires.

slides.title: Join decision workflow
slides.transcript:
Here is the workflow I want you to use whenever you build a join. First, define the grain. Before writing SQL, say out loud what one row in the final result should represent. Maybe it is one patient, one admission, one student registration, or one sales transaction. If you cannot describe the target grain clearly, the query can become confusing very quickly.

Second, identify the row sets you are combining. Third, decide the matching rule. Usually the relationship is based on a key such as patient_id, customer_id, or course_id. But do not assume that two columns with the same name automatically represent the correct relationship.

Fourth, decide which unmatched rows must stay. Suppose a public health analyst wants a list of every patient, including people with no lab results. That requirement tells you that the patient table must be preserved. If the question is only about patients who have lab results, then unmatched patients do not need to remain.

Fifth, predict cardinality. Can one patient have many admissions? Can one admission have many lab tests? Finally, validate the output. Compare what you expected with what SQL actually returned. This workflow may feel slower at first, but it prevents many of the errors that are hardest to notice later.

slides.title: Practice schema
slides.transcript:
The examples in this module use a small synthetic healthcare database. We have a patients table with one row per patient. Then we have child tables such as admissions, lab results, and prescriptions. A single patient can have no admissions, one admission, or several admissions. The same idea applies to lab tests and prescriptions.

We also have departments and medical staff, and admissions can reference an attending staff member. This gives us several realistic paths for joining tables. The dataset intentionally includes edge cases. For example, one patient may have no related activity, and the staging data may include an ID that does not exist in the official patient table. Those are not random complications; they represent the kinds of imperfect relationships analysts regularly encounter in operational data.

[tts-break]

Those edge cases are important because they let us see what different join types actually preserve. In a real project, unmatched records are often the records you care about most. A bank might want to find transactions with no matching customer. A university might want to find students with no registration record. A company might want to find products that have never been sold.

As you read the queries, keep the relationships in mind. Joining patients to admissions changes the result from patient-level data to admission-level detail. If a patient has three admissions, that patient information may repeat three times. That repetition is not automatically a duplicate problem. It reflects the structure of the data. Later, when we build department metrics and patient summaries, you will see how the same source tables can be transformed to a different grain depending on the analytical question.

slides.title: Join mental model
slides.transcript:
A useful way to think about joins is to separate two ideas: matching and preservation. The ON condition controls matching. It tells SQL when one row from the first table should be connected with one row from the second table. For example, an admission matches a patient when the patient IDs are equal.

The join type controls preservation. It answers a different question: if a row has no match, should that row disappear, or should it remain with NULL values from the missing side? This is why the same ON condition can produce different results under INNER JOIN and LEFT JOIN.

Imagine an online store. One table contains all customers and another contains orders. If we use INNER JOIN, customers without orders disappear. If we use LEFT JOIN with customers on the left, every customer stays, and customers without orders have NULL values for order columns. The matching rule did not change. The preservation rule changed.

Also remember that joins combine rows, not just unique IDs. If one customer has three orders, there are three valid customer-order combinations. Before you run a join, try to describe it in plain language: compare these two row sets, match them using this rule, and preserve these unmatched rows. If you can say that clearly, your SQL is usually much easier to design.

slides.title: Row preservation map
slides.transcript:
This slide summarizes the four main row-preservation patterns. INNER JOIN keeps only matches. If a patient has no admission, that patient will not appear in a patient-to-admission INNER JOIN. This is useful when the question is specifically about records that exist in both tables.

LEFT JOIN keeps every row from the left table. If there is no matching row on the right, the right-side columns become NULL. RIGHT JOIN does the same thing in the opposite direction. FULL OUTER JOIN keeps unmatched rows from both sides.

Try to connect each join type to a real question. In education, INNER JOIN could show only students who submitted an assignment. LEFT JOIN could show every student and their submission when one exists. FULL OUTER JOIN could compare two class rosters and reveal students who appear in only one system.

Do not rely only on Venn-diagram-style pictures. Those pictures can help, but the stronger habit is to ask, what population must remain complete? If the answer is every patient, put patients on the preserved side. If the answer is every department, preserve departments. If the answer is records from both systems, even unmatched ones, think about FULL OUTER JOIN.

slides.title: INNER JOIN
slides.transcript:
Now let us run an INNER JOIN. In this query, patients receives the alias p and admissions receives the alias a. The ON condition says that a row from admissions matches a row from patients when the patient IDs are equal.

Before running the query, make a prediction. Which patients will appear? Patients with at least one admission should appear. A patient with no admission should disappear. Also think about patients with multiple admissions. If one patient has two admissions, that patient should appear on two result rows because each row represents one matching admission.

Run the query and inspect the patient IDs and admission IDs. Try not to focus only on whether the query runs. Ask whether the number of rows makes sense. If admissions has eight valid admission records, and every admission belongs to a valid patient, the joined result should contain about eight rows.

This same pattern appears in many industries. A retailer may join customers with orders to analyze only customers who purchased something. A learning platform may join students with completed assessments to analyze only students with activity. INNER JOIN is useful when a match is required by the question.

slides.title: Aliases and grain
slides.transcript:
Aliases and grain solve two different kinds of confusion. Aliases make the SQL easier to read. If both patients and admissions contain patient_id, writing p.patient_id and a.patient_id tells us exactly where the column comes from. As queries grow to three, four, or five tables, aliases become essential.

Grain helps us interpret the result. Suppose Alice has two admissions. Her patient information may appear twice after the join. That does not mean the data is duplicated incorrectly. It means each result row represents one admission with patient information attached.

This is a very important habit: when you see repeated values after a join, do not immediately add DISTINCT. DISTINCT can hide a real modeling issue. First ask whether the repeated rows represent different valid events.

For example, if a customer places five orders, their name will appear on five order rows. If you use DISTINCT carelessly, you may accidentally remove meaningful detail. A good practice is to write one sentence before the query: one row in this result represents one admission with patient information. That sentence becomes your validation target. If the output behaves differently, you know where to investigate.

slides.title: LEFT JOIN
slides.transcript:
A LEFT JOIN is one of the most useful patterns in analytics because it allows us to preserve a clearly defined population. Here, patients is on the left. That means every patient should remain, whether or not an admission exists.

Run the query and look for a patient whose admission_id is NULL. That NULL does not mean SQL failed. It means the patient had no matching admission. In fact, that NULL may be exactly what the analyst wanted to find.

Now imagine a university retention project. One table contains every enrolled student. Another contains advising appointments. If we use INNER JOIN, students with no appointment disappear. But those students may actually be the ones we most want to identify. Using LEFT JOIN keeps the full student population and makes the missing appointment visible.

This is why preservation matters. LEFT JOIN is often the right choice when the denominator is all patients, all students, all customers, or all products. If you use INNER JOIN by mistake, inactive entities disappear and your rates or averages may become biased.

slides.title: Anti-join
slides.transcript:
An anti-join pattern answers a practical question: which rows on the left have no related row on the right? In this example, we want patients who do not have any lab results.

We start with a LEFT JOIN so every patient is preserved. If a patient has no matching lab result, the lab-side columns become NULL. Then we filter for a right-side key, such as test_id, being NULL.

The choice of column in the NULL test matters. A primary key is a good choice because a real matched row should always have that value. If you tested a column that could legitimately be NULL, you might incorrectly label a matched record as unmatched.

This pattern is extremely useful in real projects. An e-commerce company can find customers with no orders. A university can find students with no course registration. A hospital can find patients with no follow-up visit. A warehouse can find products with no sales. Read the logic in plain English: keep all left-side records, attempt the match, and then keep only the records where no right-side row was found.

slides.title: RIGHT JOIN
slides.transcript:
RIGHT JOIN is valid PostgreSQL syntax and it preserves every row from the right table. In this example, departments is on the right, so every department stays even if no medical staff member belongs to it.

If a department has no staff, the department information still appears and the staff columns become NULL. That makes it easy to identify empty departments.

In practice, many analysts prefer LEFT JOIN because it reads more naturally from left to right. We could place departments first and then LEFT JOIN medical staff. The result would be easier for many people to read because the preserved population appears first.

This is an important style lesson. SQL is not only for the computer. It is also documentation for the next analyst, developer, or data engineer who reads your work. The best join is often the one that makes the business meaning obvious. So rather than memorizing RIGHT JOIN as a special case, focus on the preservation rule: which table must remain complete?

slides.title: FULL OUTER JOIN
slides.transcript:
FULL OUTER JOIN is especially useful for reconciliation. Reconciliation means comparing two sources and making sure we can see matches as well as records that exist in only one source.

In our example, the patient master is the official table, while the staging table represents imported data. We want to see three possibilities: a patient that exists in both tables, a patient that exists only in the official master, and a staging row that has no official patient.

This same idea appears in finance when comparing two transaction systems, in human resources when comparing payroll with employee records, or in education when comparing enrollment systems with learning-platform accounts.

The CASE expression in the query helps turn those situations into readable labels such as matched, missing from staging, or missing from master. COALESCE can also help when the identifier may come from either table depending on which side is unmatched. FULL OUTER JOIN is powerful because it does not throw away evidence. When you are doing data-quality work, unmatched rows are often the rows that deserve the most attention.

slides.title: Outer join comparison
slides.transcript:
Choosing a join becomes easier when you translate the question into a preservation rule. If the question is only about patients who have admissions, then requiring a match is appropriate, so INNER JOIN fits.

If the question says every patient, whether or not an admission exists, then the patient population must be preserved. Put patients on the left and use LEFT JOIN. If the question says every department, including departments with no staff or admissions, preserve departments. If you need to compare two sources and see unmatched records from both sides, FULL OUTER JOIN is a natural choice.

Pay attention to words such as every, only matched, including those with none, and unmatched from both sides. Those phrases are clues.

For example, a manager might ask, show me every product and its total sales, including products with zero sales. That is not the same question as show me products that sold this month. The first one needs preservation of the product table. The second can require a match. SQL syntax becomes much easier when you learn to hear the preservation requirement inside the business language.

slides.title: ON vs WHERE
slides.transcript:
This is one of the most important ideas in the module. ON and WHERE are not interchangeable in an outer join. The ON clause defines which rows are allowed to match. The WHERE clause filters the final joined result.

Suppose we LEFT JOIN patients to lab results and we only want Glucose tests. If we place the Glucose condition inside ON, we are saying: every patient should remain, but only Glucose rows are allowed to match. Patients without Glucose results still stay in the output with NULL lab fields.

If we move that same condition into WHERE, the meaning changes. After the LEFT JOIN, unmatched patients have NULL in the lab test name. The condition test_name equals Glucose is not true for NULL, so those patients are removed.

This issue appears in many projects. Imagine every customer should appear, but only orders from 2026 should match. If the year condition is in ON, customers with no 2026 orders remain. If you put the year condition in WHERE, those customers disappear. The query still runs, which is why this bug can be dangerous. Always ask whether a condition controls matching or final filtering.

slides.title: Filter in ON
slides.transcript:
Now we will look at the safer pattern when we want to preserve the left-side population. The first condition in ON matches patients to lab results by patient_id. The second condition says that only Glucose rows are eligible to match.

Run the query and check the patient IDs. Every patient should still appear because the LEFT JOIN preserves the patient table. Then inspect the lab columns. Patients with a Glucose test will show test information. Patients without one will remain, but their lab fields will be NULL.

This is a very useful real-world pattern. Suppose a company wants every employee listed, along with their most recent safety training if the training was completed this year. Or a university wants every student listed, along with a tutoring visit if the visit occurred this semester. The date or category restriction often belongs in the matching logic when the population must remain complete.

Before you run the query, predict which rows should have non-null values. Then compare your prediction to the result. That habit turns SQL from trial-and-error into reasoning.

slides.title: WHERE trap
slides.transcript:
This query looks almost identical to the previous one, but the meaning changes because the Glucose condition moved from ON to WHERE.

The LEFT JOIN first creates a result that preserves patients. For patients without lab matches, the lab columns are NULL. Then the WHERE clause filters those joined rows. When it asks whether test_name equals Glucose, NULL rows do not satisfy the condition, so the unmatched patients disappear.

This is a classic SQL trap because the query is syntactically correct. PostgreSQL will not warn you. The only way to catch the problem is to understand the intended population and validate the output.

A good debugging method is to run both versions side by side. Count the distinct patients in each result. Ask which result matches the business requirement. In real analytics work, this difference can affect denominators, percentages, risk calculations, and dashboards. If the requirement says all patients, but your WHERE clause removes unmatched patients, the analysis can be systematically biased without producing any error message.

slides.title: USING
slides.transcript:
PostgreSQL offers USING as a convenient alternative to ON when both tables share the same join-key name. If patients and admissions both contain patient_id, then USING patient_id tells PostgreSQL to match those columns and return one copy of the join key in the output.

The result relationship is the same as if we had written an ON condition that compared the two patient_id columns directly.

USING can make simple joins shorter and cleaner, but ON is more flexible. Use ON when the key names are different, when you need multiple conditions, or when the relationship requires an expression.

For example, if one table uses customer_id and another uses client_id, USING cannot express that relationship. If you need to match by both account_id and date, ON is clearer. The goal is not to use the shortest syntax possible. The goal is to make the relationship obvious. Whatever style you choose, you should still be able to explain the match in one sentence.

slides.title: SELF JOIN
slides.transcript:
A self join is not a separate JOIN keyword. It is a regular join where the same table appears twice using different aliases. The aliases allow the two copies of the table to play different roles.

Here, medical staff is referenced as s1 and s2. We match staff members who belong to the same department. We also require the first staff ID to be less than the second staff ID. That second rule prevents matching a person to themselves and prevents reverse duplicates such as Alice-Bob and Bob-Alice.

Self joins are very useful when rows in one table need to be compared with other rows from the same table. In an employee table, one row might represent an employee and another row the manager. In a sales table, you could compare purchases from the same customer. In a hospital, you can compare one admission with a later admission for the same patient.

The important idea is role labeling. Before writing a self join, decide what each alias represents. Earlier event and later event. Employee and manager. First purchase and next purchase. Good alias roles make the logic much easier to understand.

slides.title: Readmissions self join
slides.transcript:
This self join uses the admissions table twice so we can compare an earlier admission with a later admission for the same patient. The patient IDs must match, because we only want admissions for the same person.

We also create an order between the two rows so that one admission plays the role of earlier encounter and the other plays the role of later encounter. That prevents reverse duplicates. Then we use the dates to keep cases where the later admission occurred within a meaningful time window after discharge.

This type of logic is common in healthcare analytics when studying readmissions, follow-up visits, or repeat procedures. The same approach could be used in retail to compare a customer's first purchase with a later purchase, or in cybersecurity to compare repeated login events for the same account.

Aliases are especially important here because both rows come from the same table. Without clear role names, the query becomes very hard to read. When building a self join, always define the roles in plain language first: earlier admission and later admission. Then translate those roles into SQL.

slides.title: CROSS JOIN
slides.transcript:
CROSS JOIN creates every possible combination between two row sets. Unlike a normal join, there is no ON condition restricting the matches.

Suppose we have two departments and three appointment slots. A CROSS JOIN creates six combinations: each department paired with each slot. In this case, that may be exactly what we want.

Cross joins are useful for building schedules, scenario grids, test cases, calendars, and completeness frameworks. For example, a retailer could create every store and every day of the month so they can later identify days with no sales. A university could create every course and every expected assessment type to find missing assessments.

But the growth can be dramatic. If one table has ten thousand rows and the other also has ten thousand, the result can have one hundred million combinations. Before running a cross join on large data, estimate the size by multiplying the row counts. Cross joins are not bad; accidental cross joins are bad. Use them when the combinations are intentional.

slides.title: Cross join growth
slides.transcript:
Cross joins make cardinality very easy to see because the multiplication is direct. Two rows crossed with three rows produce six result rows. One hundred crossed with one hundred produces ten thousand. Ten thousand crossed with ten thousand produces one hundred million.

That same multiplication can happen in ordinary joins when several rows on each side share the same key. The difference is that it may be less obvious.

Imagine a customer has three orders and four support tickets. If you join both detail tables directly to the customer by customer_id, you can create twelve order-ticket combinations for that customer. Those twelve rows do not mean twelve new business events. They are combinations created by the join.

Whenever your result becomes much larger than expected, do not immediately assume the database is wrong. Ask whether the join created combinations. Check how many matches each key has on both sides. Cardinality is one of the most important concepts in analytical SQL because it explains many surprising row counts.

slides.title: Cardinality
slides.transcript:
Cardinality describes how many rows can match a key. In a one-to-one relationship, each key matches at most one row on both sides. Those joins are usually easy to reason about.

In a one-to-many relationship, one patient may match several admissions. The patient information repeats once for each admission, and that can be perfectly correct.

The risk appears when we join several one-to-many child tables at the same time. Suppose one patient has two admissions, two lab tests, and two prescriptions. If all three tables are joined independently by patient_id, we can create two times two times two, or eight, combinations.

This idea applies everywhere. One customer can have many orders, many support tickets, and many website sessions. One student can have many courses, many submissions, and many advising visits. If you join all of those detail tables together without thinking about grain, counts can become inflated.

Before aggregating, predict the relationship type for each join. If the final result should be one row per parent, consider summarizing each child table to the parent grain before joining.

slides.title: Row multiplication
slides.transcript:
This runnable example makes row multiplication visible. We join patients to admissions, lab results, and prescriptions, all by patient_id. Each child table can have multiple rows for the same patient.

Focus on a patient who has several records in more than one child table. The final joined row count can be much larger than the number of admissions, lab tests, or prescriptions that actually occurred.

COUNT star counts the joined combinations. That is why it can look surprisingly large. COUNT DISTINCT admission_id, COUNT DISTINCT test_id, and COUNT DISTINCT prescription_id are trying to recover the number of original events from the multiplied result.

In a real project, this can create serious reporting errors. Imagine a hospital dashboard that reports the number of admissions after admissions are joined to several lab and medication tables. If COUNT star is used carelessly, admission volume can be exaggerated. The query is not broken. It is counting something different from what the analyst intended.

Whenever a count looks too large, ask what one joined row represents. That question often reveals the problem immediately.

slides.title: COUNT trap
slides.transcript:
COUNT star is not wrong. It counts rows exactly as requested. The problem is that the rows after a complex join may not represent the event you think they represent.

If one joined row represents a combination of one admission, one lab test, and one prescription, then COUNT star counts combinations. It does not directly count admissions, lab tests, or prescriptions.

COUNT DISTINCT can sometimes protect a measure. For example, counting distinct admission IDs can recover the number of admissions even after other detail tables are joined. But DISTINCT should not become a magic repair tool. You still need to understand why the multiplication happened.

Often the clearest solution is to pre-aggregate. Summarize admissions to one row per patient, summarize labs to one row per patient, and summarize prescriptions to one row per patient. Then join those summaries.

This is a useful real-world habit: name the measure explicitly. Are you counting patients, admissions, orders, products, sessions, or joined row combinations? Once the measure is clearly named, the right counting strategy becomes easier to choose.

slides.title: Pre-aggregate first
slides.transcript:
This query shows one of the safest patterns for analytical joins. Instead of joining every detail row first, we summarize each child table before the join.

The admission-count CTE produces one row per patient. The lab-count CTE also produces one row per patient. The prescription-count CTE does the same. Only after those sources are at the same grain do we join them to the patient table.

Now the final result is easy to defend: one row per patient. Patients with no activity remain because we use LEFT JOIN, and COALESCE converts missing counts to zero.

This pattern is very common in dashboards. Suppose a customer dashboard needs total orders, total support tickets, and total returns. A safe design is to summarize each activity table by customer first, then join the summaries to the customer master. The SQL is a little longer, but the result is much easier to validate and explain.

In analytics, a slightly longer query that clearly protects the target grain is usually better than a shorter query that produces ambiguous counts.

slides.title: Validation checklist
slides.transcript:
A join should be validated before its result is used in reporting, analysis, or machine learning. Start with row counts. How many rows were in each input table, and how many are in the output? A sudden increase or decrease may be expected, but you should be able to explain it.

Next, count distinct keys. If the final result should have one row per patient, compare COUNT star with COUNT DISTINCT patient_id. If those numbers are different, investigate why.

Inspect keys with unusually many matches. A patient with five admissions or ten lab tests is useful for understanding the join behavior. Also spot-check at least two known cases: one entity with multiple related records and one entity with no related record.

Finally, write the grain sentence. For example: one row represents one patient with summarized activity counts. If you cannot write a clear sentence describing one result row, the query may still be logically unclear.

This validation process is simple, but it catches a large share of real-world join problems before they reach a dashboard, report, or executive decision.

slides.title: Multiple joins
slides.transcript:
Now we combine several tables in one query. The first join moves from patients to admissions using patient_id. Because the result is at admission detail, using INNER JOIN is reasonable if we only care about admissions that belong to valid patients.

The second join moves from each admission to the attending staff member using attending_staff_id. Here we use LEFT JOIN so the admission can remain even if the staff reference is missing.

Notice the path: patient to admission, then admission to staff. That path matters. We are not joining tables just because they have columns that look similar. We are following documented relationships.

This is exactly how larger real-world queries should be designed. For example, in retail the path might be customer to order, then order to payment. In a university it might be student to registration, then registration to course. Write the relationship path before writing the SQL.

Also keep checking the grain. Adding the staff table should not create more admission rows if each attending staff ID points to at most one staff member. If the row count increases unexpectedly, that is a signal to investigate the relationship.

slides.title: Protect target grain
slides.transcript:
A correct-looking join key can still be wrong if it does not match the level of the relationship. Suppose your target result is one row per admission. You already have patients joined to admissions correctly.

Now imagine adding lab results using patient_id only. If one patient has multiple admissions and multiple lab tests, every admission can pair with every lab result for that patient. The admission grain is no longer protected.

The deeper question is: what does the lab record belong to? Does it belong to the patient generally, to a specific admission, or to a specific encounter? The database design should tell you. If the true relationship uses encounter_id, joining only on patient_id is too broad.

This mistake happens in many domains. A customer ID may appear in orders, payments, and support tickets, but that does not mean every payment belongs to every order. A student ID may appear in registrations and grades, but the correct relationship may also require course_id and term.

Before adding a table, restate the target grain and ask whether the new table is at the same level. If not, aggregate it, filter it, or use a more specific key.

slides.title: Guided practice 1
slides.transcript:
For this guided practice, the goal is department-level performance. The requirement says every department must appear, even departments with no admissions or no staff. That tells us the departments table should be the preserved population.

We LEFT JOIN admissions and medical staff to departments. Because a department can have several admissions and several staff members, the detail rows can multiply. That is why the counts use DISTINCT event identifiers.

Run the query and look for the department with zero activity. It should still appear. That is an important validation of the LEFT JOIN. Then inspect a busy department and compare the counts with the underlying records.

This style of query is common in management dashboards. A company may want every region listed, even if a region had zero sales. A university may want every academic program listed, even if no students enrolled this term. The dashboard should not make zero-activity groups disappear.

Read the query in sections: preserved table, first relationship, second relationship, grouping level, and measures. Breaking a long query into those logical pieces makes it much easier to understand.

slides.title: Guided practice 2
slides.transcript:
This practice is about explaining row multiplication, not just running the SQL. Focus on one patient who has several admissions, lab results, and prescriptions.

If those three child tables are all joined by patient_id, each admission can combine with each lab test and each prescription. That is why the number of joined rows can be much larger than the number of original events.

A strong explanation should use the word combinations. The query is not creating new admissions or new lab tests. It is creating combinations of existing rows because several one-to-many relationships are being joined at the same time.

Compare this with the pre-aggregation strategy from the earlier slide. When each child table is summarized to one row per patient first, the multiplication disappears.

Do not memorize a rule such as always use DISTINCT. Instead, identify the target grain and the cardinality of every relationship. That reasoning is transferable to other projects such as customer analytics, educational analytics, finance, and operations. Whenever several detail tables connect to the same parent, row multiplication should be one of the first things you check.

slides.title: Guided practice 3
slides.transcript:
The business question here is: list all patients and show Glucose tests when they exist. The words all patients are the most important part of the requirement. They tell us that the patient population must remain complete.

Run the query with the Glucose condition inside ON. You should see every patient. Patients with Glucose tests will have lab values. Patients without a Glucose test will remain with NULL lab fields.

Now imagine moving the same condition into WHERE. The result becomes a different population: only patients with Glucose tests. This is not just a syntax difference. It changes the meaning of the analysis.

The same idea appears in many projects. A retailer may want every product and its sales from a specific month when sales exist. A university may want every student and a tutoring visit from this semester when one exists. If the optional condition belongs to the matched data but the full population must remain, ON is often the correct place.

Try to explain the difference using two ideas: ON limits eligible matches. WHERE filters the final joined rows.

slides.title: Project timeline
slides.transcript:
This project combines joins with skills from earlier modules. We first create a common event structure by stacking admissions, lab tests, and prescriptions with UNION ALL. Each source is transformed into the same basic shape: patient ID, event date, event type, and event details.

Once the event stream is created, we join it to patients so every event can include the patient's name.

This pattern is useful because we define the grain clearly before the join. One row in the event CTE represents one event. The join enriches each event with patient-level information without changing the event grain.

Real-world systems often use this idea to build timelines. A customer journey might combine purchases, website visits, support calls, and returns. A student activity timeline might combine logins, assignment submissions, advising appointments, and course registrations. A security timeline might combine login attempts, alerts, and account changes.

Run the query and inspect one patient across several dates. Try to follow the story created by the events. SQL becomes much more meaningful when you can connect the rows to a real analytical narrative.

slides.title: Project transitions
slides.transcript:
This project combines join reasoning with a window-function idea. Inside the CTE, LEAD looks forward within each patient's admissions ordered by date. That gives us information about the next admission, including the next department and the next admission date.

The outer query then keeps cases where a next department exists and where the department changes. Finally, it groups the transitions to summarize how often patients move from one department to another.

Even though the final logic is not a traditional join, the same grain thinking applies. Inside the CTE, one row represents one admission plus information about the following admission. After grouping, one row represents one transition pair, such as Emergency to Cardiology.

This type of analysis appears in many fields. In retail, you might study transitions from one product category to another. In education, you might study students moving from one course level to the next. In operations, you might study workflow steps. The key habit is to keep restating the grain after every major transformation.

slides.title: Assessment concepts
slides.transcript:
Before the coding exercises, make sure you can explain the core ideas in your own words. First, why can a LEFT JOIN followed by a WHERE condition on the right table remove unmatched left rows? Your explanation should mention that unmatched right-side values become NULL and that WHERE filters the final joined result.

Second, can you choose a join type from the population rule? Only matched records suggests INNER JOIN. Every patient suggests preserving patients with LEFT JOIN when patients are on the left. Reconciliation across both sources suggests FULL OUTER JOIN.

Third, can you explain row multiplication without simply calling the extra rows duplicates? Several child tables with multiple matches can create combinations. The rows may be unique as combinations even though they inflate event counts.

Finally, can you design a one-row-per-patient result safely? A strong answer is to summarize each child table to patient grain before joining it to the patient master.

If you can explain these ideas clearly, the syntax becomes much easier. The goal is not memorization. The goal is reasoning about the data structure and the business question.

slides.title: Assessment coding strategy
slides.transcript:
This slide shows the main coding strategy behind the final exercises. The target is one row per patient with three measures: admission count, lab count, and prescription count. Patients with no activity must still remain.

The safest solution is to aggregate each child table by patient_id first. After aggregation, each summary contains at most one row per patient.

Then we LEFT JOIN those summaries to patients. Because the patient table is preserved, patients with no activity stay in the result. COALESCE turns missing counts into zero.

This approach is very common in production analytics. Imagine a customer dashboard with order count, support-ticket count, and refund count. Instead of joining raw order rows, raw ticket rows, and raw refund rows together, summarize each activity first. Then combine the summaries.

Run the query and validate at least two patients: one with multiple activities and one with no activity. If the final result is one row per patient and the counts match the source data, the grain is protected.

slides.title: Exercise 1 INNER JOIN
slides.transcript:
This is Coding Exercise 1. Your task is to return patients who have admissions. The output needs patient ID, patient name, admission ID, diagnosis, and department.

The wording tells you that a match is required. We are not trying to keep patients with no admissions. That points toward INNER JOIN.

Start with patients as p and admissions as a. Ask what connects them. The relationship is patient_id. Then select the requested columns and sort the result so it is easy to inspect.

Do not try to force one row per patient. The correct grain is one row per matching admission. If a patient has three admissions, that patient should appear three times.

Before using Run and Check, predict whether any patient will disappear. After running, compare the number of rows with the number of admissions. If the query runs but does not pass, inspect the grain, selected columns, and matching condition before randomly editing syntax.

slides.title: Exercise 2 LEFT JOIN
slides.transcript:
Coding Exercise 2 changes the population rule. This time, every patient must appear, even if the patient has no admission. The phrase every patient tells you which side must be preserved.

Patients should be on the left side of the join, and admissions should be optional.

Before running the query, predict what an unmatched patient should look like. The patient ID and patient name should still have values. The admission ID and diagnosis should be NULL because no admission row matched.

After Run and Check, find that unmatched patient in the result. Also notice that patients with multiple admissions still appear multiple times. LEFT JOIN preserves the patient population, but it does not force one row per patient.

This is a useful distinction. Preservation and grain are related, but they are not the same thing. A LEFT JOIN can keep every patient and still return several rows for patients with several admissions.

slides.title: Exercise 3 Anti-join
slides.transcript:
Coding Exercise 3 uses the anti-join pattern. You need to return patients who do not have any lab results.

Start by preserving all patients with a LEFT JOIN. Then attempt to match lab rows. For patients with no lab result, the lab-side columns become NULL.

Now choose a right-side column that cannot be NULL for a real matched row. The lab test ID is a good choice because it is a primary identifier. Filter for that key being NULL.

Read your query as a sentence: keep all patients, try to match lab results, then keep only the patients for whom no lab result was found.

This anti-join pattern is common in real data-quality work. Find customers with no purchases, employees with no required training, students with no submission, products with no inventory record, or patients with no follow-up visit. Once you understand the pattern, you will use it often.

slides.title: Exercise 4 ON vs WHERE
slides.transcript:
Coding Exercise 4 checks whether you understand the difference between matching and final filtering. The requirement says every patient must remain, while only Glucose lab rows should be allowed to match.

That tells you the Glucose condition belongs in the matching logic.

Complete the ON clause and do not move the test-name condition into WHERE. Before running the query, predict the shape of the result. Every patient should appear. Some patients will have a Glucose test ID and value. Others will have NULL lab fields.

After Run and Check, inspect both types of rows. If only patients with Glucose tests remain, then the full patient population was not preserved.

The purpose of this exercise is not just to pass the checker. It is to build a habit. Whenever you use an outer join, ask whether each condition belongs to the match or to the final result filter. That decision can change the meaning of the analysis.

slides.title: Exercise 5 Safe counts
slides.transcript:
Coding Exercise 5 is the most important cardinality exercise in the assignment. The required grain is one row per patient. You need admission count, lab count, and prescription count, and patients with no activity must still remain.

Do not directly join all three detail tables and then use COUNT star. That creates combinations and can inflate the measures.

Instead, summarize each child table by patient_id inside the common table expressions. Each summary should return one row per patient with one count. Then LEFT JOIN those summaries to the patient table.

Use COALESCE or another missing-value fallback so a patient with no activity shows zero instead of NULL.

After Run and Check, validate the result. The number of output rows should equal the number of patients. Check one patient with several activities and one patient with no activity. This exercise represents a pattern you will use often in dashboards and reporting systems where multiple measures must be combined safely at one target grain.

slides.title: Exercise 6 Department metrics
slides.transcript:
The final coding exercise combines preservation, cardinality, and aggregation. The result must contain one row per department, including departments with zero activity.

Start from departments because that is the population to preserve. LEFT JOIN admissions by department and LEFT JOIN medical staff by department.

Because one department can have several admissions and several staff members, the combined rows can multiply. If you count rows directly, the measures may be inflated. Use distinct identifiers when counting admissions and staff.

Then GROUP BY department so the final grain is one department per row.

After Run and Check, find the department with no activity. It should still appear with zero counts. Then inspect a busy department and make sure the counts reflect real admissions and real staff, not the multiplied join combinations.

This is very similar to real management reporting where every region, team, program, or product category must appear even when activity is zero.

slides.title: Complete Module
slides.transcript:
This is the final completion page for Module 6. The module tracks ten knowledge checks and six coding exercises. Before selecting Complete Module, review the counters and make sure they represent the work you intended to finish.

If an activity is incomplete, the page will list it and allow you to return to the relevant slide.

When you select Complete Module, the page creates a Canvas submission summary. That summary includes your completion status, knowledge-check answers, and the SQL saved for each coding exercise.

Review that summary before copying it. If the module is incomplete, the page will warn you before you copy the current progress.

Remember that progress is stored locally in the current browser. If you switch computers, use a private browsing window, or clear browser storage, the saved work may not follow you.

Treat this page as a final quality-control step. In data work, reviewing the output before submitting or publishing is just as important as writing the query itself.

slides.title: Summary
slides.transcript:
Let us summarize the major ideas from Module 6. Start with grain. Decide what one result row should represent before writing the join.

Then think about preservation. INNER JOIN keeps only matches. LEFT JOIN and RIGHT JOIN preserve one designated side. FULL OUTER JOIN preserves unmatched rows from both sides.

Remember that ON controls matching while WHERE filters the joined result. This difference is especially important with outer joins.

Cardinality explains why rows repeat or multiply. One-to-many repetition can be perfectly correct, but several one-to-many child tables joined together can create combinations that inflate counts.

When your target is one row per patient, customer, student, or department, pre-aggregating child tables is often the clearest solution.

Finally, validate. Compare total rows, distinct keys, unmatched cases, and known examples. If you keep one habit from this module, let it be this: define the grain, predict the matches, run the join, and verify the result before trusting it. That workflow will help you far beyond this course.

slides.title: Next: Subqueries
slides.transcript:
The next module moves from joins to subqueries. A join combines row sets directly. A subquery allows one query to use the result of another query as part of its logic.

You will see subqueries used for questions such as: which patients have an admission above the average length of stay, which customers have at least one large order, or which products have never appeared in a sales table.

The join skills from this module still matter. When deciding between a join, a subquery, or a common table expression, continue asking about grain, cardinality, and clarity.

Before moving on, make sure you can explain the difference between matching and preservation, and make sure you understand why several detail tables can multiply rows. Those two ideas will continue to appear in more advanced SQL.

As SQL becomes more expressive, the goal is not to use the most advanced syntax. The goal is to write logic that is correct, understandable, and easy to validate.
